verified_clean: BrowserWindow flags, stated plainly (src/main/index.ts:40-47): contextIsolation TRUE (explicit, :42), nodeIntegration FALSE (explicit, :43), preload path :41, backgroundThrottling false :46. `sandbox` is NOT set — Electron >=20 default is true and nothing here disables it (no nodeIntegration:true). `webSecurity` is NOT set — default true. `allowRunningInsecureContent`, `nodeIntegrationInSubFrames`, `webviewTag` all unset (defaults). A repo-wide grep for sandbox|webSecurity|nodeIntegration across src/ returned exactly one hit: index.ts:43.

Express server bind address is loopback-only and explicit: mcp-server.ts:118 `srv.listen(port, '127.0.0.1', ...)` — not 0.0.0.0, on both the DEFAULT_PORT (38473, :16/:127) and the ephemeral fallback (:129). The advertised URLs are built from `http://127.0.0.1:${port}` (:133).

No process spawning anywhere in the privileged surface: grep for `child_process|execSync|spawn(` across all of src/ returned zero hits. No IPC channel takes a command, argv, or shell string — the full channel list (shared/ipc-types.ts:1-38) is file read/write/stat/list, two dialogs, three recent-project ops, and a perf log line.

No shell.openExternal, no custom protocol registration, no registerFileProtocol/interceptFileProtocol, no <webview> — grep for `openExternal|registerFileProtocol|protocol.|<webview` across src/ returned zero hits. The renderer loads only ELECTRON_RENDERER_URL in dev (index.ts:50-51) or a local `loadFile` in prod (:53).

A real CSP ships with the renderer: src/renderer/index.html has `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data: blob:` — no unsafe-inline on scripts, no remote origins.

The /aether loopbackOnly middleware is genuinely restrictive for the route it covers (mcp-server.ts:83-91): the regex is anchored (`^(127\.0\.0\.1|localhost|\[::1\]|::1)(:\d+)?$`), so Host `127.0.0.1.evil.com` fails, Origin `null` (sandboxed iframe / file://) fails, and a missing Host fails. Its weakness is scope (A1), not the check itself.

guarded-write.ts is the one write path that is both atomic and genuinely guarded, and its guard is tested with a real violating input: every relPath is checked with isRelPathSafe before ANY write (:59-63, throws), the conflict check is all-or-nothing before the first write (:67-78), and each file is written tmp-then-rename in the same directory (:89-93). test/main/guarded-write.test.ts:30-35 plants `relPath: '../escape.bin'` and asserts `rejects.toThrow(/unsafe project-relative path/)` — a guard that actually asserts something.

isRelPathSafe (src/shared/rel-path.ts) rejects the real escape shapes: leading `/`, leading `\`, `^[a-zA-Z]:` drive letters, and any `..` segment split on both separators. It has its own test file (src/shared/__tests__/rel-path.test.ts). Its four consumers in file-io.ts (readManyFiles :25, pathExists :46, fileMtime :63, listDir :78) all call it before touching the fs.

agent-bridge.ts request lifecycle is leak-free on all three exits: resolve/reject via the response listener clears the timer and removes the 'closed' listener (:26-32); the timeout path deletes the pending entry and removes the 'closed' listener (:53-59); the window-closed path deletes and clears the timer (:46-52). Pre-flight checks reject on destroyed/loading webContents (:38-43) so a request can never be sent into a dead renderer.

Both dialog handlers scope themselves to the sender's own window (ipc-handlers.ts:57, :97, :111 via BrowserWindow.fromWebContents) and return null/false on cancel, so file:save can only write to a path the user picked in a native dialog (:119-121).

The MCP tool surface and the Aether method surface cannot drift: both are generated from the single EDITOR_METHODS array (mcp-server.ts:33 loop; aether/adapter.ts:24-25 maps). Aether params are validated with the same zod shapes before forwarding (adapter.ts:68-71), and unknown methods are rejected (:66). The JSON-RPC envelope handling correctly distinguishes notifications (id absent → null response) from requests throughout.

file:read-binary's missing-file marker round-trip is correct end to end: main resolves `{__missing}` for ENOENT only (ipc-handlers.ts:24-26), and the preload rethrows it as an ENOENT-shaped Error (preload/index.ts:10 → ipc-types unwrapBinaryRead), with isMissingFileMarker explicitly excluding ArrayBuffer views so a legitimate byte payload can never be mistaken for the marker.
The CDP debug port is env-gated and loopback-bound (index.ts:25-28): nothing opens a remote-debugging port unless AURORA_DEBUG_PORT is set, and the address switch pins 127.0.0.1.

findings.title: /mcp has no Host/Origin guard while /aether does — the stated D8 protection is bypassable via a sibling route with identical capability
findings.claim: The express MCP route POST /mcp is registered with no middleware, while POST /aether and GET /aether/events are wrapped in `loopbackOnly`; both surfaces dispatch the exact same EDITOR_METHODS registry, so the Host/Origin check is a no-op defense.
findings.evidence: mcp-server.ts:65 `exp.post('/mcp', async (req, res) => {...})` — no middleware argument. Contrast mcp-server.ts:97 `exp.post('/aether', loopbackOnly, ...)` and :107 `exp.get('/aether/events', loopbackOnly, ...)`. The guard itself is at :83-91 and checks `req.headers.host` / `req.headers.origin` against a loopback regex. The comment at :81-82 claims the Aether surface is protected by "loopback bind + Origin/Host check, never remotely exposed (protocol D8)" — but the MCP route exposes the same methods: buildServer() at :33 iterates `EDITOR_METHODS` (editor-methods.ts:47-157), the same array the Aether adapter maps at aether/adapter.ts:24-25. Transport is constructed at mcp-server.ts:68 with only `{ sessionIdGenerator: undefined }`; the SDK's own DNS-rebinding protection is available and not enabled (node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/server/webStandardStreamableHttp.d.ts:84 allowedHosts, :90 allowedOrigins, :96 enableDnsRebindingProtection). Failure scenario: user has Aurora open; visits attacker.com, which rebinds to 127.0.0.1. The page is then same-origin with the server (no CORS preflight at all), and POSTs to http://attacker.com:38473/mcp with Host: attacker.com. /aether would return 403 'loopback only (protocol D8)'; /mcp accepts. The page then calls tools open_project{dir:'/home/<user>/sonic_hacks/s1disasm'} → edit_chunk/edit_block/set_layout_region → save_project. save_project reaches agent-handler.ts:729-731 `saveClassicProject()` with no confirmation dialog, writing the mutated act through the guarded channel (the mtime guard passes, because Aurora itself holds the current baselines). Net: the user's disassembly is silently rewritten on disk.
findings.fix: Apply `loopbackOnly` to the /mcp route the same way as /aether (mcp-server.ts:65), and/or construct StreamableHTTPServerTransport with `enableDnsRebindingProtection: true, allowedHosts: ['127.0.0.1:'+port,'localhost:'+port], allowedOrigins: [...]`. Belt-and-braces: both.

verdict.reasoning: Could not refute; every link traced independently. (1) mcp-server.ts:65 registers POST /mcp with no middleware — grep for `loopbackOnly` across src/ yields only the definition (:83) and the two /aether routes (:97, :107); the sole app-level middleware is express.json (:62). (2) The transport does not compensate: mcp-server.ts:68 passes only `{ sessionIdGenerator: undefined }`, and the installed SDK v1.29.0 defaults protection off — node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/dist/esm/server/webStandardStreamableHttp.js:70 `this._enableDnsRebindingProtection = options.enableDnsRebindingProtection ?? false`, with validateRequestHeaders (:107-109) short-circuiting when false. (Note: the seat cited the .d.ts; the .js confirms the same defaults.) (3) Identical capability: buildServer() iterates EDITOR_METHODS (mcp-server.ts:33) and aether/adapter.ts:24-25 maps the same import, so edit_chunk/edit_block/set_layout_region/save_project are reachable from /mcp. (4) No handshake gate: server/index.js has no "not initialized" rejection for inbound requests, so a cold tools/call on a per-POST stateless server succeeds; transport preconditions are only Accept: application/json + text/event-stream (:378) and Content-Type: application/json (:382), all freely settable on a same-origin fetch from a rebound page. (5) The write lands unconfirmed: agent-handler.ts:729-731 `case 'classic-save-project': requireClassicProject(); return saveClassicProject();` — no dialog, in contrast to classic-open-project at :574-584 which explicitly fails closed because an agent-driven call "has no UI to confirm through". (6) Unconditional exposure: src/main/index.ts:64 starts the server on app.whenReady() with no flag; mcp-server.ts:118 binds 127.0.0.1:38473. Concrete trigger: Aurora running with an s1disasm project open; attacker serves a page on http://attacker.com:38473 that DNS-rebinds to 127.0.0.1, then same-origin POSTs {jsonrpc:"2.0",method:"tools/call",params:{name:"edit_block",...}} then {name:"save_project"} to /mcp with Host: attacker.com:38473 — /aether would 403 at :89, /mcp accepts. Unverified link (stated honestly): whether a 2026 browser still permits the rebound public-origin -> loopback fetch under Chrome's Local Network Access tightening. That is an external mitigation applying equally to /aether, not a property of this code, so it lowers exploitability without making the missing guard correct.
verdict.severity_correction: Stated severity "high" is correct — hold it. Not critical: the silent on-disk mutation requires an active attacker plus a browser that still allows rebinding-to-loopback, so it does not fire under normal use the way genuine silent-corruption bugs do. Not lower than high either: a fully write-capable route sits beside one explicitly guarded against exactly this threat, under a comment (mcp-server.ts:81-82) claiming the surface is "never remotely exposed (protocol D8)" — a real hole in a stated protection, not a theoretical one.

findings.title: file:write-binary is the only write channel with no rel-path guard, and one caller interpolates an unsanitized free-text name into the path
findings.claim: WRITE_BINARY_FILE resolves the renderer-supplied relativePath against basePath with no isRelPathSafe check and mkdirs parents recursively, so an absolute or `..`-bearing path writes anywhere the user can write — and the sprite export path builds that string from an unsanitized UI text field.
findings.evidence: ipc-handlers.ts:81-94: `const fullPath = resolve(basePath, relativePath); mkdirSync(dirname(fullPath), {recursive:true}); writeFileSync(tmpPath, ...); renameSync(...)`. No `isRelPathSafe` anywhere in the handler — compare WRITE_GUARDED (ipc-handlers.ts:52-54 → guarded-write.ts:59-63, which throws on an unsafe relPath) and the read/probe helpers (file-io.ts:25, :46, :63, :78). ipc-types.ts documents the guard only for FILE_MTIME/WRITE_GUARDED ("Both are fully rel-path-guarded on the main side"); WRITE_BINARY_FILE is silently outside that claim. Reachable path: SpriteMode.tsx:219 renders `<input ... value={spriteName}>` bound to the sprite store name; SpriteMode.tsx:146 calls `exportSprite(spriteName)`; export-sprite.ts:70,93 build `const dir = `${spritesDir()}/${name}`` and then write `${dir}/${name}_anims.asm` (:98), `${dir}/mappings.bin` (:95) etc. The module HAS a sanitizer — export-sprite.ts:151 `sanitizeName()` strips everything outside [A-Za-z0-9_] — but it is applied only to import-side names (:163 nameFromPath, :453, :509), never to the export name. Concrete input: type `../../../s1.asm` (or `../../../../.bashrc`) into the sprite-name field and press Export → main mkdirs and writes outside the project with no error. Even the benign case `Sonic/Run` silently creates a nested directory the sprite index will not find again.
findings.fix: Add `if (!isRelPathSafe(relativePath)) throw new Error(...)` at the top of the WRITE_BINARY_FILE handler (ipc-handlers.ts:82), matching guarded-write.ts:59-63; and apply `sanitizeName()` to the export name in export-sprite.ts:70 before it is interpolated into the path (guarding the caller alone is not enough — the channel is the boundary).

findings.title: The editor bus has no authentication at all; the discovery file publishes the port to every local process
findings.claim: Neither /mcp nor /aether requires any token, and Aurora advertises its port in a world-readable file in the user's home directory, so any local process can drive the full editor surface and rewrite the user's disassembly unattended.
findings.evidence: No auth middleware exists anywhere in mcp-server.ts — the only middleware is `loopbackOnly` (:83-91), which authenticates nothing (it inspects Host/Origin, headers any non-browser client sets freely). mcp-server.ts:132-153 writes `~/.aurora/mcp.json` AND `~/.sonic-level-editor/mcp.json` via `writeFileSync(p, contents)` with default mode (0644 &~umask), containing `{url, port, pid, aether, aetherEvents}` (:134-141). Worst three calls for a hostile local process (e.g. a postinstall script in any repo the user builds): (1) `open_project {dir}` (editor-methods.ts:108-110) → `edit_chunk`/`edit_block`/`set_layout_region` (:118-126) → `save_project` (:155-156); save_project reaches agent-handler.ts:729-731 `saveClassicProject()` with no prompt, so the disasm is corrupted on disk in one round trip. The mtime guard in guarded-write.ts does not help — Aurora holds the matching baselines. (2) `set_colind` (:142-144) / `set_level_palette` (:149-151) / `place_object` (:133-135) — subtle data mutations the user won't see until a build breaks or collision goes wrong. (3) `screenshot` (:103-105) exfiltrates the editor viewport as PNG, and `get_project_info`/`get_project_report` (:48, :111) leak absolute project paths and a file inventory. The only friction is open_project's unsaved-work refusal (agent-handler.ts:579-584), which is defeated by simply waiting for a clean state. This is a stated posture ("Trusted local-developer API", mcp-server.ts:81-82) — the finding is that the comment names loopback+Origin as the protection, and that protection covers neither local processes at all nor the /mcp route (see A1).
findings.fix: Generate a random token at startup, include it in mcp.json, write mcp.json with mode 0600, and require it as a bearer header on both /mcp and /aether. If that is rejected as too heavy for a dev tool, at minimum correct the comment at mcp-server.ts:81-82 so no future reader believes the surface is authenticated, and gate the destructive classic methods (save_project, set_layout_region, edit_block) behind an explicit opt-in env var.

findings.title: file:read-binary and file:list-project-files are unguarded — the renderer has arbitrary filesystem read
findings.claim: readBinaryFile does no path validation, so an absolute or `..` path escapes the project root; listProjectFiles likewise walks any basePath. The rel-path guard is therefore a hygiene convention, not a security boundary.
findings.evidence: file-io.ts:5-8 `readBinaryFile(basePath, relativePath) { const fullPath = resolve(basePath, relativePath); return readFile(fullPath); }` — no isRelPathSafe, unlike readManyFiles (:25), pathExists (:46), fileMtime (:63), listDir (:78). ipc-handlers.ts:17-28 wires it straight through. This is deliberate and load-bearing: three renderer call sites pass basePath `''` plus an absolute path — chunk-library-import.ts:42-44, import-sheet.ts:48 `readBinaryFile(path, '')`, export-sprite.ts:157-158 `readAbsolute()` whose own comment says "selectFile returns absolute paths". So the exception cannot simply be removed. listProjectFiles (file-io.ts:96-115, wired at ipc-handlers.ts:30-32) takes basePath verbatim and recursively walks it (bounded only by MAX_DEPTH 10 / MAX_FILES 50000). Concrete input: `window.api.readBinaryFile('', '/home/<user>/.ssh/id_ed25519')` returns the key bytes to the renderer. Realistic exposure is low — contextIsolation is on, the CSP in src/renderer/index.html is `default-src 'self'`, and no remote content is loaded — so this needs renderer code execution first. Stated so nobody assumes the guard is a sandbox.
findings.fix: Split the channel: keep `file:read-binary` guarded with isRelPathSafe, and add an explicit `file:read-absolute` used only by the three dialog-derived call sites, so the escape hatch is visible and enumerable instead of ambient on the main read path.

findings.title: No setWindowOpenHandler / will-navigate handler — a child window would inherit the preload and expose window.api on a remote origin
findings.claim: createWindow installs no navigation or window-open policy, so Electron's defaults apply: window.open to an arbitrary URL is allowed and the child window inherits the parent's webPreferences including the preload that exposes arbitrary file read/write.
findings.evidence: src/main/index.ts:32-59 is the entire window setup — webPreferences (:40-47) sets only preload, contextIsolation, nodeIntegration, backgroundThrottling. The only listeners registered in the whole main process are `win.on('closed')` (:56), `app.on('activate')` (:66), `app.on('will-quit')` (:73), `app.on('window-all-closed')` (:75). A repo-wide grep for `setWindowOpenHandler|will-navigate|web-contents-created|openExternal|registerFileProtocol|<webview` returned zero hits across src/. The CSP at src/renderer/index.html (`default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'`) does not restrict top-level navigation or window.open. Failure scenario requires prior renderer code execution: `window.open('https://attacker.example')` yields a window whose webPreferences are inherited from the parent, i.e. the same preload, so the attacker page gets `window.api.readBinaryFile` / `writeBinaryFile`. Nothing in the app currently opens external URLs (no window.open, no target=_blank in src/renderer), so this is hardening-only today.
findings.fix: In createWindow: `win.webContents.setWindowOpenHandler(() => ({ action: 'deny' }))` and `win.webContents.on('will-navigate', (e, url) => { if (!url.startsWith(expectedOrigin)) e.preventDefault(); })`.

findings.title: Second Aurora instance clobbers then deletes the discovery file, orphaning the first instance
findings.claim: The discovery file is written unconditionally and deleted unconditionally on quit, so running two Aurora instances leaves the surviving one undiscoverable.
findings.evidence: mcp-server.ts:125-130: if port 38473 is taken, `listen(0)` picks an ephemeral port. :142-153 then writes `~/.aurora/mcp.json` and the legacy path with the new port, overwriting whatever the first instance wrote — no check for an existing live entry. stopMcpServer (:157-163) `rmSync(p)` on every path in discoveryPaths, unconditionally. Sequence: instance A starts on 38473 and writes mcp.json; instance B starts, falls back to an ephemeral port, overwrites mcp.json with B's port; B quits → will-quit (index.ts:73) → stopMcpServer deletes mcp.json; A is still listening on 38473 but no bus client can discover it. Second scenario: any crash/kill of Aurora leaves a stale mcp.json pointing at a dead port, and a later unrelated process binding 38473 would receive bus traffic aimed at Aurora.
findings.fix: Include the pid in the file (it already is) and refuse to overwrite when the recorded pid is alive; on stop, delete only if the file's pid matches process.pid.

findings.title: recent-projects.json shape is never validated; a non-array file breaks the recents API with a TypeError
findings.claim: getRecentProjects catches parse errors but not shape errors, so a corrupt store containing valid JSON that is not an array makes addRecentProject/removeRecentProject throw, rejecting the IPC invoke.
findings.evidence: recent-projects.ts:16-21 `return JSON.parse(data)` inside try/catch — the catch covers SyntaxError only; a file containing `{}` or `null` is returned as-is, typed (falsely) as RecentProject[]. addRecentProject:28 then calls `projects.filter(...)` → `TypeError: projects.filter is not a function` for `{}`, or a throw on `null`. That propagates out of ipcMain.handle (ipc-handlers.ts:73-75) as a rejected invoke; the renderer's recents UI has no repair path, and every subsequent project open re-throws. Also writeFileSync at :36 and :43 is uncaught, so a read-only or full userData dir turns every project open into a rejected invoke rather than a soft failure.
findings.fix: `const parsed = JSON.parse(data); return Array.isArray(parsed) ? parsed.filter(p => p && typeof p.path === 'string') : [];` and wrap both writeFileSync calls in try/catch that returns the in-memory list.

findings.title: Bus-facing paint/stamp methods have unbounded size params while their siblings are capped
findings.claim: paint_region's w/h/entries and set_layout_region's chunkIds carry no upper bound, unlike every neighbouring method, so a local bus client can hand the renderer an arbitrarily large region.
findings.evidence: editor-methods.ts:68 `paint_region` params: `w: z.number().int().min(1), h: z.number().int().min(1), entries: z.array(entrySchema)` — no `.max()` on w/h and no `.max()` on the array. Compare get_nametable_region (:56, w/h max 64), paint_collision (:76, w/h max 128), get_tiles (:53, count max 256), write_tiles (:65, max 128), set_bg (:96, tiles max 512). editor-methods.ts:119 `set_layout_region` chunkIds is `z.array(z.array(...))` with no length bound. Both schemas are the single validation gate for both transports (aether/adapter.ts:25 builds `z.object(m.params)` from the same shape; mcp-server.ts:36 passes it as inputSchema). Concrete input: `{"method":"editor/paint_region","params":{"section":0,"x":0,"y":0,"w":1000000,"h":1000000,"entries":[...]}}` under the 16mb body limit (mcp-server.ts:62) — the renderer iterates w*h. Worst case is a hang/OOM of the editor, i.e. loss of unsaved work.
findings.fix: Add `.max(...)` bounds to paint_region w/h and entries and to set_layout_region's grid, consistent with paint_collision's 128 cap.

findings.title: SSE subscriber set is unbounded, and the advertised event channel is never actually pushed to
findings.claim: addSubscriber accepts unlimited SSE connections with no cap and no auth, and `broadcast` — the only thing that would use them — is never called anywhere in the codebase, so the advertised editor/ready event stream emits exactly one message at connect time and nothing thereafter.
findings.evidence: mcp-server.ts:107-113 registers every GET /aether/events connection via `addSubscriber(res)` (adapter.ts:86-88, a plain `Set.add`) with no limit; removal happens only on `req.on('close')`. A local process opening connections in a loop grows the set without bound. Separately, `broadcast` (adapter.ts:94-99) is exported but a repo-wide grep for `broadcast(` finds only its own definition at adapter.ts:94 — no caller in src/. capabilities() at adapter.ts:36 advertises `events: ['editor/ready']`, and the only editor/ready ever sent is the inline literal at mcp-server.ts:111 written directly into the response at subscribe time. So a client that subscribes and waits for state-change events waits forever.
findings.fix: Cap the subscriber set (and drop oldest on overflow), and either wire broadcast() into the store's change notifications or stop advertising an events capability that nothing emits.
